questions.q: According to this lesson, what's the core problem with a pre-production security checklist kept only as a wiki page or document?
options: It can be skipped under deadline pressure, since nothing actually enforces that each item was checked before a merge or deploy happens
Documents cannot list more than five items
It automatically expires after 30 days and must be rewritten
Wiki pages cannot describe CI/CD concepts accurately
questions.explain: A document nobody is forced to consult gets skipped when a deadline is tight. The fix is expressing the same checklist as CI jobs that are marked as required status checks, so the gate is structural rather than something people remember to do.

questions.q: Which of these belongs on the pre-production checklist as a direct carryover from the least-privilege lesson in this chapter?
options: The repository's README has been spell-checked
Every commit message follows a specific emoji convention
CI/CD permissions are explicit and minimal, and fork-triggered jobs run on a pool with no access to production secrets
The project's logo has been updated to the latest brand guidelines
questions.explain: Lesson 26 covered scoping CI tokens to a permissions block and separating fork-triggered jobs from production-deploy runners — both carry forward directly as checklist items in the pre-production gate.

questions.q: Why does the checklist specifically call for dependency and base-image versions to be pinned, rather than left on a floating tag like latest?
options: Pinned versions make builds faster to download regardless of network conditions
Floating tags are rejected by every package registry automatically
Pinning has no real effect and is included only as a style preference
A pinned version makes exactly what shipped reproducible and auditable, instead of a floating tag that can resolve to different content on different builds
questions.explain: A floating tag like latest can point to different actual content over time. Pinning an exact version or digest means the same build input always produces the same result, and you can later say with certainty what was actually in a shipped artifact.

questions.q: In the example GitHub Actions configuration, what makes the secrets-scan and sbom-and-scan jobs actually block an unsafe merge, rather than just running informationally?
options: Naming the jobs in all capital letters
Marking them as required status checks in the repository's branch protection settings, so GitHub won't allow the merge button to be clickable until both pass
Running them on a schedule instead of on pull_request
Adding a comment in the YAML file explaining that they are important
questions.explain: A workflow job running in CI is only informational unless branch protection is configured to require its success. Marking secrets-scan and sbom-and-scan as required status checks is what turns them into an actual, un-bypassable gate.

questions.q: What does the checklist's audit-trail requirement specifically ask for after a deploy?
options: A record of who approved the deploy, which commit SHA shipped, and where that build's SBOM and scan reports are stored
A public announcement posted to social media after every deploy
A new SBOM generated once per fiscal quarter instead of per build
Deleting all CI logs immediately after a successful deploy to save storage
questions.explain: The audit-trail item is about attributability: knowing who approved the release, exactly which commit was deployed, and where the corresponding SBOM and vulnerability scan results for that specific build can be found later.
